strengths: Addresses a timely and important privacy vulnerability in agentic multi-modal LLMs during their rapid deployment
Novel problem formulation: first systematic investigation of inference-stage privacy leakage through image geolocation
Clear and well-structured methodology with comprehensive empirical analysis of 50 privacy-sensitive images
Concrete findings with street-level accuracy (60% within 1 mile) and systematic identification of critical visual cues for geolocation
Thorough categorization of 30+ visual elements contributing to location inference with targeted occlusion experiments
Realistic threat model based on actual doxing scenarios from public social media
Excellent presentation with detailed example interactions demonstrating model reasoning process
weaknesses: Dataset size of only 50 images is insufficient for strong statistical claims and generalizability to broader population
Exclusive focus on ChatGPT o3 without evaluation on other agentic multi-modal models (GPT-4V, Claude, Gemini), limiting understanding of generality
Severely limited geographic scope (only major U.S. cities + few international locations) reduces applicability to different urban architectures and regions
Missing critical baselines: no human performance comparison, no comparison with simpler geolocation methods, no model component ablations
Incomplete evaluation of defense mechanisms: only one detailed masking experiment shown; insufficient systematic evaluation of obfuscation effectiveness
No statistical rigor: lacking confidence intervals, significance testing, cross-validation, or hold-out test sets
Reproducibility impossible: dataset not publicly available (even anonymized), limited prompt engineering details, no code released
Limited technical novelty: primarily an empirical security audit without new methods, algorithms, or theoretical contributions
Insufficient prompt sensitivity analysis: Figure 3 shows different prompts but lacks systematic ablation study on prompt effects
Incomplete ethical treatment: limited discussion of responsible disclosure timeline or broader societal implications of findings

strengths: Identifies important, timely, and overlooked privacy vulnerability in MLRMs with clear legal/policy implications (GDPR/CCPA)
Comprehensive evaluation across 11 diverse models (open/closed-source MLRMs and MLLMs) with multiple metrics and settings
High-quality, carefully curated DOXBENCH dataset (500 images) addressing key gaps in existing Street View-based datasets with three-level privacy framework
Novel and well-motivated evaluation metrics: VRR appropriately captures refusal behavior; GLARE is theoretically grounded information-theoretic measure combining multiple dimensions
Strong analytical insights: 98% human agreement on clue-based reasoning; CLUEMINER extracts 102 interpretable clue categories; clear evidence models lack privacy-aligned mechanisms
Realistic threat modeling with GEOMINER collaborative attack framework and human-model comparisons (15-21× better performance)
Honest assessment of defense limitations with clear mechanistic analysis of failure modes
Well-written paper with clear visualization and solid organization
weaknesses: Limited geographic scope (California only, 6 cities) with unclear generalization to other regions/countries; raises concerns about regional bias in model training interactions
Modest dataset size (500 images) and methodological concerns: only 5 human participants, no confidence intervals/significance testing, IQR filtering without justification
Concurrent work (refs [3-5], [21-22]) addresses similar location-leakage problems; while differentiation is meaningful, core novelty is somewhat incremental
CLUEMINER limitations: depends on GPT-4O for category analysis (potential bias), applied only to correct predictions (selection bias), no inter-annotator agreement validation
Tool-augmented evaluation based on only 10 manually selected 'challenging' cases per risk level—may not be representative and could overstate threat severity
Defense discussion lacks depth: only one guardrail tested, no post-training fine-tuning strategies discussed, utility-privacy tradeoffs not fully quantified, no forward-looking solutions
DOXBENCH not publicly available limiting reproducibility; code availability not mentioned; confined to those with model API access
Statistical rigor issues: no formal significance testing, selection biases in subgroup analyses (e.g., mirror cases only 46 images), Top-K evaluation somewhat artificial
